job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Felix Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the plant by seven. Cartonajes Levante makes cardboard boxes outside Valencia, and I plan the maintenance: which machine gets serviced when, and which spare parts we order. I do it in an Excel sheet and by walking the line with Joaquín, the fitter who has been here thirty years. I finished mechanical engineering last summer with a plain pass and no internship, and my final project was a gearbox for a conveyor. I share a flat with Hugo, a friend from university, and we play football on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. Machines break, people fix them, and a computer doesn't change a bearing. At work Joaquín would say he told me so over coffee. I wouldn't say much online, I'm not someone who posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good for me. My job planning repairs on the corrugator, the machine that makes the cardboard, stays as it is. I'd still have a loan of 9,000 euros and a rent share of 400, but everyone needs boxes, so a quiet year at the plant suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep planning maintenance in my Excel sheet and walking the line with Joaquín twice a day. I'd save 200 euros a month and pay the loan a bit faster. I'd maybe take the forklift licence, since it's useful whether AI exists or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. A bit sleepy, if I'm honest. I like it when nothing is new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing differently from today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much nothing. In a year I'd ask for a pay rise and a proper contract instead of the graduate one. My supervisor Pilar says the plant is doing fine, but I'd like it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joaquín mostly, he's fifty-eight and has fixed every machine in the building. And Hugo, my flatmate, who works at a car parts firm. We complain about our bosses and then watch football.

I'd say little online, since I'm not someone who posts.
think: Planning repairs on the **corrugator** stays as it is, which is good for me.
Everyone needs boxes, so a quiet year suits me, though the **9,000 euro** loan stays.
do: Keep planning maintenance in Excel and walking the line with **Joaquín** twice a day.
Save **200 euros** a month and pay the loan faster.
feel: Content and a bit **sleepy**, since I like it when nothing is new.

fieldNote: Content with routine; plateau confirms his belief that **machines need people**.
Wants a pay rise and a **proper contract**, in writing.
Social circle is small: Joaquín and Hugo.

steps.text: Keep planning maintenance in Excel and walking the line with Joaquín
Put 200 euros a month toward paying off the loan
Take the forklift licence course in the spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. People get excited about software, and then it breaks. At work I'd say the planning sheets are fine, and if Pilar buys a program to do them I'll check it. I wouldn't say much to friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, scheduling and ordering spare parts is thinking work, and it's about half my job. If a program does that, Pilar may not need a planner. Walking the line and fixing things stays with Joaquín and the fitters. I'd be a planner without plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the hands-on side better: take a hydraulics course and spend more time with Joaquín learning to fix things. I'd save 250 euros a month. I'd not touch the AI tools unless the plant forced me, and then I'd learn only what they require. If they cut planners I'd ask to move to the fitters' team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like not knowing what Pilar is thinking. It's like waiting for a machine to jam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't touch the AI tools. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust what I can't open up and look at. With a machine I can take it apart and see why it failed, but a program that tells me what to order, I can't open. And if I follow it and the line stops, I'm the one who gets the call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hugo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the safe place is the shop floor. He's in an office at a car parts firm and does exactly the paperwork that software loves. I'd tell him to learn something with his hands, maybe weekend electrics. He'd laugh, and then check his CV.

say: I'd say we'll see, because people get excited about software and then it **breaks**.
At work I'd say the sheets are fine, and I'd **check** any program Pilar buys.
think: Scheduling and ordering parts are about **half my job** and could go to software.
I'd be a planner without plans, with the fitting side staying with Joaquín.

fieldNote: Resistance is rooted in **inspection**: he trusts what he can open and check.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening hydraulics course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should slow it down. At work I'd say nothing, because Pilar would be thinking the same. I'd probably go and talk to my dad, who runs a small tile shop in Alzira, because he'd have a view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning part goes in two years, I think. Then I'm a graduate with a plain pass and no tool skills, in a plant that might not need a planner. I'd still have the hands-on part until about 2031, but then robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Pilar to move me onto the shop floor as a fitter's assistant and learn the machines. I'd save 350 euros a month and give up the gym. I'd ask my dad if I can work at the shop at weekends if things go badly. I'd probably go home to Alzira rather than pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I plan maintenance for a living, so not knowing what's coming is the hardest part for me. I don't sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of not knowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody in charge knows either. If Pilar knew the plan I could follow it, but she'd be guessing, and so would the owners. Following a plan is what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad's shop need from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He needs someone to do the invoices and the website, which I'd hate but could do. He'd rather I stayed at the plant, but he'd take me in a heartbeat. He's old school: family first, pride later.

say: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should **slow it down**.
I'd say nothing at work, and talk to my dad in Alzira.
think: The planning part goes in **two years**, leaving a plain-pass graduate with no tool skills.
Hands-on work lasts until about 2031, then robots come.
do: Ask Pilar to move me to the **shop floor** as a fitter's assistant.
Save **350 euros** a month and give up the gym.
Work weekends at my dad's tile shop, or move home to Alzira.
feel: Anxious because not knowing what's **coming** is the hardest part, and I sleep badly.
S2.quote: I plan maintenance for a living, so not knowing what's coming is the hardest part for me.
fieldNote: Anxiety comes from **lack of a plan**, not from fear of machines.
Family fallback is concrete: his dad's tile shop and a home in Alzira.
Resistant to tools, so he moves toward the work robots reach last.

steps.text: Ask Pilar for a fitter's assistant post on the shop floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say it's worth keeping an eye on. At work I'd ask Pilar if the plant has a plan. I wouldn't change anything out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have time. By 2031 I'd be 27, with a proper contract and the hydraulics course. The planning gets done by software, but the plant still needs people on the floor until 2034. I'd work on being someone who can fix things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the hydraulics and electrical maintenance course in the evenings and save 250 euros a month. I'd learn the plant's planning software once Pilar buys it, but only the part I need. I'd still avoid the chatty tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a long maintenance shutdown: you know it's coming, you can prepare, but you don't enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the planning software after all. What's the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Pilar would have chosen it and I'd be trained on it, not chasing it on my own. If the plant brings in a system, I'll learn the buttons. What I won't do is go looking for new tools myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Pilar didn't buy anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, then I'd keep my sheets. A job on paper is only as safe as the paper, so I'd still do the course, because someone who can fix a machine always has work.

I wouldn't change anything out loud.

The plant still needs people on the floor until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say the world will have sorted itself out. At work I'd say nothing and keep my head down. I'd think a lot about my pension, which is a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be 32 and a maintenance lead who knows the machines, which is something no program does. Robots might come in 2039, but I'd be the one who looks after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, take the hydraulics course and save 200 euros a month. I'd think about a flat of my own in Valencia. I'd start learning the new tools once they're proven and everyone else uses them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like ten years. It's long enough that I stop thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plant might be sold, and that worries me more than any program, because I can't do anything about it. A small family firm can't afford new machines, but a big group could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the plant look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer people, more machines, same noise. I'd be the guy with the toolbox and a tablet that tells him what's wrong. I'd learn the tablet then, when it's proven, not before.

I'd think about my **pension**, which is a long way off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I like plans and there'd be none. I'd have a loan, a pass degree and a planning job a program can do. What would help is a company that says honestly what it'll do and a government that pays for a trade course. It would also help if my dad's tile shop in Alzira stays open, since it's my back-up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against new things, I'm against being first. Let someone else test it, and when it works I'll learn it. I'd rather fix a machine properly than be the first to try a new one.

headlineQuote: I'm not against new things, I'm against being first. Let someone else test it, and when it works I'll learn it.
portrait: **Felix**, 22, plans maintenance at a cardboard box plant near Valencia, with a plain mechanical engineering degree and a loan to repay.
A centrist who dislikes drama, he trusts things he can **take apart** and avoids AI tools entirely.
His planning and ordering work is the exposed part; his **hands-on** side with Joaquín is his insurance.
He stays calm when little changes and gets anxious in the 2028 world, where he'd have **no plan** to follow.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because he likes plans and there would be none.
whatWouldHelp: A company that says honestly what it will do, and public money for a **trade course**.
His dad's tile shop staying open as a **back-up**.
